sections.overview: Despite its common name, Drosophila melanogaster is a vinegar fly in the family Drosophilidae, not a tephritid true fruit fly. Its short generations and well-studied genetics made it a landmark model for studying animal heredity and development.
sections.identification: Adults are about 3 millimetres long, with females slightly larger than males. The thorax bears six legs and clear forewings; small knob-shaped halteres, the altered hindwings, help stabilize flight. Wild-type flies have reddish eyes and a yellow-brown body with dark abdominal bands; the male’s abdomen is darker toward the rear. In one laboratory study, mean wet mass was 0.693 ± 0.050 mg for females and 0.505 ± 0.047 mg for males; mass depends on rearing conditions and is not a fixed field measurement.
sections.habitat: Originally African, it now occurs worldwide. It gathers where fruit, plant juices and other foods ferment, from orchards and markets to kitchens and restaurants.
sections.diet: Larvae and adults exploit fermenting fruit together with its yeasts, bacteria and other microbes; the patch supplies microbial food as well as a suitable place for young flies to develop.
sections.behavior: Adults often gather around fermenting food. During courtship, a male follows and taps a female, vibrates one wing to sing, then licks her before attempting to mate; she may reject him. The exchange combines sound, touch and chemical cues.
sections.reproduction: After mating, the female stores sperm and lays successive fertilized eggs on suitable decaying food; she can lay roughly 400 eggs over time. At about 25 °C in standard laboratory conditions, eggs hatch in roughly a day; larvae feed and moult twice through three stages, then pupate before adults emerge. This egg-to-adult cycle takes about ten days under those laboratory conditions. Females may become receptive to mating within about 8–12 hours of emergence, depending on temperature.
sections.ecology: By feeding and breeding in decomposing fruit, flies ingest microbes and return them to the substrate in their droppings, helping maintain a shared fruit–microbe–fly community and carrying microbes between temporary patches of decay. Yeasts and bacteria do not just share the patch: they shape its food value and microbial conditions for the next brood.
sections.conservation: The species is globally widespread and commonly gathers in homes, restaurants and other places where food is served, where people often regard it as a nuisance.
